title: AAA 4 - The Live AMA
summary: Recording of a live livestream Q&A covering learning strategy, getting hired, building a portfolio, reading documentation and course-roadmap news. No code is taught; the takeaways are career and study advice.

concepts.heading: Learning and languages
points: Treat programming languages as tools rather than school subjects: pick up whichever one the current project needs instead of mastering one fully first. An iOS app goal does justify getting solid in Swift first.
Mixing up syntax when switching languages is normal; lean on a good code editor and its linting/syntax highlighting for the mechanical part and spend your own effort on logic.
Learn by defining a concrete goal, splitting the topic into the parts that goal needs, then practising those parts repeatedly. Avoid trying to memorise a whole reference (every method of an API).

Information is cheap to look up, so skip memorising documentation. Search for a worked example (often Stack Overflow), spot the method used, then read the official docs for background as needed. Documentation quality varies a lot between vendors.

concepts.heading: Getting a developer job
points: Competition exists for any desirable role; focus on the goal and on becoming good enough to be hard to ignore rather than watching other applicants.
Think from the hiring manager's side: they receive huge numbers of applications and have little time, so visible proof of ability beats listing qualifications.

Build a portfolio of real projects that go beyond tutorial material. A suggested idea is to clone a tool a manager uses daily (a task board like Trello, for example) and add your own feature that addresses a pain point, so the reviewer instantly grasps its value.
Apply the same perspective-taking to any goal that involves other people.

concepts.heading: Building projects and starting out
points: Moving from tutorials to independent building requires struggle; the 100 Days of Code course deliberately reduces hand-holding over time (fewer videos, more docs and Google use) to build that independence, ending in your own portfolio projects.
Start small and grow a project step by step rather than aiming at a huge product at once.
For a startup there is no perfect moment: find spare time alongside current work, and expect chances to come from earlier preparation.
Young learners can try freelance marketplaces: charge very low prices first to gather reviews and experience, then raise the rate as demand grows.
Involve UI/UX design from the start of a project, not at the end; try many apps and note which experiences you like.
Pricing software: depends on appeal and niche size; broad-appeal products can be cheaper, niche ones need higher prices to cover development time.

concepts.heading: Course roadmap notes (as of the stream)
points: No separate new iOS course planned; the existing iOS course was to receive updates, with a gradual shift toward SwiftUI while UIKit stays the job-relevant skill.
No Java course planned. Python and JavaScript are both viable for web work; the instructor sees no single 'most powerful' language.

pitfalls: Content is conversational and time-sensitive (2020 context); the iOS/SwiftUI remarks may be out of date.
Nothing here is required for the coding curriculum.
